artboards.title: Today — a clock and a line about the house
A — a row of glance cards along the bottom
B — the one line opens into a ledger
C — the clock left, ranked cards right
A2 — glance cards, the fact as the big type
B2 — the ledger at across-the-room size (chosen)
D — A's layout without the cards

annotations.text: Today, from App.vue: after three minutes the wall rests to the sky and five centered lines of type. It is calm, but it says very little. "Something is on in 2 rooms" does not say which, and does not say it is warm inside or that music is still playing in the kitchen. A household walking past has to wake the panel to find out anything, and waking it drops them on Home rather than on what they wanted to know.

A, the reference photo. The clock takes the top left, the weather the top right, and four equal cards run edge to edge along the bottom: Home, Lights, Climate, Music. A card is drawn only for something the house has. Music is there only while something plays; when nothing does, its place goes to Next, the soonest routine. A tap on a card wakes the panel onto that thing rather than onto Home. This says the most, and it is the one that looks most like a product. It is also the brightest at 3am, so after bedtime the cards dim with the sky.

B keeps today's centered wall and adds no new surfaces. The one line about the house opens into a ledger of four short facts with an icon each, and the weather moves up to share the date's line. Lamp color marks the fact that is live. This reads as a clock first and a dashboard never, and it is the one that sits best in a dark bedroom corridor. Its limit is length: every fact has to fit in two or three words, and there is nothing to tap except the whole screen.

C is ranked like the Rooms bento. The clock and weather hold the left half. On the right, the thing most worth knowing leads as a large card (here the music, with its cover), and the rest follow as rows: lights, the warmest room, the house, the next routine. The lead card changes with the house. A door left unlocked, somebody at the door, or a phone asking to join would take it over. This carries the most information without looking busy, but it is the most work to build and needs a ranking rule the house agrees with.

Round two, 28 September. A and B were close, but the status has to read from across the room, not only when standing in front of the wall. In A and B the fact was 16 to 19px of prose beside an icon. Here the fact is the big type: one or two words at 52 to 76px (Calm, 3 on, 21°, Playing), with the where below it at 21 to 22px, which is still readable from a few steps away. The clock gives up some size to pay for it.

A2 keeps A's cards and makes them taller, with a 64px figure in each. It is the closest to the reference photo. The cards give every fact a clear edge and a place to tap, but four slabs of glass on the wall all night is a lot of surface for a screen at rest.

B2 keeps B's centered clock with a 52px ledger under it. It is the calmest of the three, and everything sits in one block the eye finds at once. Four facts at this size fill the width, so a fifth (Next, a door) has to replace one rather than join them.

D sits between the two: A's layout with B's restraint. There are no cards. Each fact stands on the sky under a hairline rule, with a small label above, a 76px figure, and the where below. It has the largest status type of the three and the least chrome, and the rule over Lights turns lamp-colored while something is on. It relies on the sky being dark enough behind the bottom third, which the resting veil already ensures.
